#Fees Must Fall- again

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Students nationally rejected Minister of Higher Education Dr Blade Nzimande's announcement that it is up to the Universities to decide on the fees increase for 2017 but says that it must be capped at 8%.He said parents earning under R600 000 annually should pay the 2015 fees but richer students should pay an increase. He acknowledged that Universities are cash strapped. The National Student Financial Aid Scheme will cover the R2.6 billion shortfall.

Summary:
Cape Town, Stellenbosch and Wits students all came out in protest saying there should be no fee increase and made a number of demands that education should be de-colonized, workers should be paid a minimum wage of R12 000 and suspended students should be allowed back onto campus. WE will watch events emerge over the week speaking to Vice Chancellor Max Price, Adam Habib as well as students leaders and education commentators

Press Release:


Universities on a Knife-Edge
Almost a year after the #feesmustfall campaign brought campuses to their knees, universities have again braced against student backlash, violent protests and nationwide campus chaos. After a 2016 fee hike freeze, this week Minister Blade Nzimande announced universities should individually determine their fee increases—capped at eight percent for 2017. Carte Blanche investigates the future of South African universities and meets brave students determined to complete degrees while living hand-to-mouth.


Script:


Script: It’s been another week of violent clashes between students and police with arrests and injuries across the country. Stun grenades, teargas, and rubber bullets have been fired as students y continue to protest for free and equal education. It all began on Monday Minister of Higher Education Blade Nzimande made this announcement
Blade ” To ensure that such inflation-linked fee adjustments on the 2015 fee baseline are affordable to financially needy students‚ government is committed to finding the resources to support children of all poor‚ working and middle class families – those with a household income of up to R600 000 per annum – with subsidy funding to cover the gap between the 2015 fee and the adjusted 2017 fee at their institution.
Script: Minister Nzimande put the ball squarely back in the Universities court saying it was up to their how they would handle their financial problems. UCT’s Vice Chancellor Max Price said they remain in the hot seat
Max Price: “Because we’re setting the fees, the vice-chancellors are in a sense hung out to dry because we have no other source of money. So we are ending up being in the frontline of that
Script: The breakthrough was acknowledging that parents are who earn between R150 000 to R600 000 who do not qualified under the National Student Financial Aid Scheme and known as the missing middle are also struggling. Their fees remain pegged at 2015 rates with the government would cover the universities increase of up to 8%
Link “Minister Nzimande’s announcement on Monday was generally welcomed as a good compromise by the various university administrations, the students however were having none of it
Script: Students immediately came out in protest at WITS UCT and Pretoria, spreading across the country as the week unfolded. Student leader Fasiha Hassan, general secretary of the WITS SRC explains the student’s anger
Hassan “the demand as it stands now of the protest is for free and quality education, the state has attempted to shift focus from the greater issue they have tried to say we have covered the increment for the missing middle the issue is solved
Script: But this makes no difference to Bathelomew Chabalala 3rd year teaching student
Bathelomew “I raise money for registration but I don’t have money for accommodation I have accommodation I don’t have food I go back to Pretoria I struggle with transport
Script: This is why these students will not compromise over free education
Bathelomew “if you don’t get proper assistance you will remain poor, you can get a NSFAS and NSFAS gives you R50 000 WITS wants R110 000 .My 3 years was like a prison to me …because my fees are being taken care of which is the most important thing, now the transport to go to Shosenguve every day using a taxi every month is R2800 I am failing to raise R100 how can I go to Shosengue
Script: Bathelomew is an orphan and has no documentation relating to his parents and so getting any assistance from the state has been a nightmare
Bartholomew “I knocked on different doors I went to ANC to Luthuli House they fail to give me assistance rather to send me to all different places, it was like a game
Script: Bathelomew only hope is to rely on support of private individuals and charities
Bathelomew “they claim that WITS is a public institution but how can we pay such incredible amounts on a public institution”
Script: Acting Vice Chancellor of WITS Prof Twana Kupe says we have to create a new funding structure
Prof Twana Kupe “we are considered high quality institutions because of the education we offer but it costs, that is why partly our fees are high also given the under- funding . So what we need to design in SA is a system where you say if you are going to fund a student is poor in kind you must fund them in full because if you don’t do that you undermine their capacity to succeed”
Hassan “it is not opening up access to education if I am paying tuition and accommodation it its easily R100 000 to R120 000 base per year, and then if I am on NSFAS when I graduate I must pay back NSFAS I have black tax I must support my mother my father, there is an obligation on me to liberate and uplift my society which is fine but then I must also pay back a loan
John “ Is it even viable to have no fee increase”
Prof Twana Kupe “I can assure you we are not viable and we are not sustainable beyond 6 months one of our key sources of income is fees, now by saying it is fees I am not sitting here and saying anybody including those who can’t pay should pay “
Script: This is true for universities across the country, Manie Regal the University of the Western Cape’s Executive Director Finance and Services
Regal “the University of the Western Cape now only has two months’ worth of operating costs if there is no funding available
Script: Elements within the protests have become violence which has lost them public support. Last year Universities across the country have spent nearly 500 million rand of valuable cash repairing damages and securing the safety of other students and property
Regal “We incurred 46 million Rands worth of costs as a consequence of the protests, and then in 2016 we have incurred about 30 million Rands worth of costs just to mitigate the risk of further damage to the institution
Hassan “the only time the general SA populous listen or hears is when something is burnt and there is something fundamentally flawed that someone feels the need to burn so desperate a building or some sort of infrastructure to be heard “
Script: And it’s a complex issue because although the fight is essentially for the poorest of the poor they are the ones that suffer the most from the shutdowns. National Student Financial Aid Scheme beneficiary Charmone Ludolph was a caught in the cross fire at UWC last year
Charmone: “A lot of students are frightened by the protests, so some people are very scared to speak up because you know there are people using violence against them, so what a lot of people are doing they are fighting over Facebook,
Script: This week UWC has been remarkably calm but they fear it could change over night
Charmone “It is very stressful and frustrating, you are working so hard, and at the end you can’t even see the result of it, all the effort you have been putting in because, you just, don’t end up writing exams.
Script: And it’s not just the damage to infra-structure
Prof Twana Kupe“. There are a number of SA now watching what is happening in the education sector might say I have the means to do this I am sending my children to Harvard , or Cambridge or some other university abroad we can’t afford to do that we need the leading environment for learning. It is a global matter we compete with other universities globally
Script: What started out as largely a peaceful protest became increasingly violent as police and private campus security intervened, which in turn fuelled student’s anger and destruction of property. At WITS on Tuesday, after a march through the streets tear gas was fired on students as they made their way back to campus
Hassan “what triggered yesterday’s events there was an ordinary student someone who was not involved in the protest trying to excite the building she came out and got involved in a battle and we watched private security physically with a baton hit .Students then reacted and said absolutely not …..and that was when there was an altercation private security pushed us back and you know there are stairs student started to fall down the stairs and that’s when the whole mess evolved… all that was seen was the latter part and not the context that what happened before
Link “One of the allegations about these protests is that there is a group that believes in tactical violence that has infiltrated the protest and that at times has caused a great deal of confusion
Script: At UCT the day started out with blockades and peaceful protest but later in the day as more people came onto campus who were not students and classes were systematically shut down. This law ethics class footage went viral
John: Do students still have the moral high ground?
Max ” Shutting down the campus, or disrupting the lectures, preventing what I do believe is the vast majority of students who want to continue studying, who want to write their exams – preventing them from doing that is infringing other peoples’ rights, intimidating them to participate, I think that’s unacceptable
Link “This is the scene in Jorrison street in Braamfontein, one side of the road has been closed off there is police helicopter circling overhead and police are maintaining a visible presence here on the street
Hassan “When we are able to express ourselves constructively you will find less violence, this kind of suppression is not helping anyone”
Link “With the fees commission months away from delivering any sort of recommendations it’s hard to know where the common ground lies between government the university and the students especially now that the rallying cry appears to have become free education or no education
John: So what is the impact of the shutdowns, what is the cost and to whom?
Prof Twana Kupe “we are at a very sensitive stage where students are almost completing their academic lectures tests and related and then we enter exams if this continues that has a very negative impact . It can kick down the academic program somebody who should have completed this year now completes next year when doctors that should have qualified this year can’t qualify and qualify next year it’s a real shortage in a real hospital or in a real clinic when communities need that service so you are impacting on so any things that are vital to the sustainability of our society
Hassan “What we need is the commission to speed up its report back. May of 2017 is far too late 100’s of 1000 of students will again in January have the doors of higher learning closed. Students want to know implementation time lines. Does it mean in 2018 we are going to be piloting a model, does it mean 2019 full roll out we need to discuss those time lines so we can hold government accountable.
Bartholomew “really I do have big dreams it is something that made me to be hungry to go to university it was because of those dreams
Charmone “Some people are right at the end of their degrees, they are in their third year, they are waiting to get it over and done with, and now they just can’t, so I think that is really sad as well
Bartholomew ”If the university were shut down like this then next year the fortunate will continue what about me”
